ci-two-means-s1.title: Spaced versus massed practice
ci-two-means-s1.text: Twenty-eight student volunteers learned 50 new vocabulary words. They were randomly assigned, 14 to each group, to study in four short sessions spread over a week (spaced) or in one long session (massed). A week later each took the same recall test (invented data).

plot.label: Side-by-side boxplots of words recalled: spaced practice centered higher than massed practice, both roughly symmetric with no outliers

ci-two-means-s2.title: Commute times in two cities
ci-two-means-s2.text: A researcher took independent random samples of commuters who drive to work in two large cities and recorded one-way commute times in minutes (invented data). Both samples are small shares of the cities' commuters. She wants to estimate $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, the difference in true mean commute time (city 1 minus city 2).

table.caption: Summary statistics of commute times, in minutes

items.q: Which procedure estimates how much better spaced practice is, on average?
options: A paired t interval for the mean difference
A two-sample z interval for $p_S - p_M$
Two one-sample t intervals, one per group
A two-sample t interval for $\mu_S - \mu_M$

why.correct: Parameter: $\mu_S - \mu_M$, the true mean recall with spaced practice minus with massed practice, for volunteers like these. Procedure: a two-sample t interval.
options: The volunteers were not paired: each was in one group only, so there are no natural pairs to subtract.
Words recalled is quantitative, so the parameter is a difference of means.
Two separate intervals do not estimate the difference, and overlapping intervals are hard to judge.
Two separate groups from random assignment, a quantitative response and unknown population standard deviations: a two-sample t interval for the difference in true mean recall.

items.q: Each group has only 14 students. How is the normal/large sample condition met?
options: The two groups together have 28 students
Neither boxplot shows strong skew or outliers
The volunteers were randomly assigned to the two groups
14 is less than 10% of the students at their school

why.correct: Conditions: random assignment (random); no 10% check for an experiment; normal/large sample from the two boxplots, each without strong skew or outliers.
options: Each group is checked on its own, and 14 is less than 30.
With $n < 30$ in both groups, each group's graph must show no strong skew and no outliers. Both boxplots are roughly symmetric with no outliers.
That is the random condition. Shape is a separate check.
The 10% condition does not apply to random assignment, and it is about independence, not shape.

items.q: How many degrees of freedom does technology give for the two-sample t interval? (The conservative choice is also accepted.)

why.correct: Technology uses the Welch formula and gives $\text{df} = 25.58$. The conservative choice is the smaller $n - 1$: $14 - 1 = 13$. Either is accepted on the exam. Reading Table B, use the row at or below the technology df (25), never a rounded-up row.

mistakes.why: That is the total number of volunteers. A two-sample t interval uses the technology df (25.6) or the conservative df, the smaller $n - 1 = 13$.
That is $n_1 + n_2 - 1$. A two-sample t interval uses the technology df or the smaller of $n_1 - 1$ and $n_2 - 1$.

That rounds the technology df up. Read Table B at the row at or below the technology df ($25.58$, so row 25), never above it. (26 is also $n_1 + n_2 - 2$, the pooled df, a method this course does not use.)

items.q: Construct the 95% confidence interval for $\mu_S - \mu_M$, in words recalled.

why.correct: $(\bar{x}_S - \bar{x}_M) \pm t^*\sqrt{\frac{s_S^2}{n_S} + \frac{s_M^2}{n_M}} = (34.21 - 28.50) \pm 2.057\sqrt{\frac{6.13^2}{14} + \frac{6.97^2}{14}} = 5.71 \pm 5.10$, from 0.61 to 10.81 words ($t^* = 2.057$ at df 25.6; the Table B row for df 25 gives 2.060 and nearly the same interval). On the exam the conservative df 13 is also accepted: $t^* = 2.160$ gives 0.35 to 11.07. Using $z^* = 1.96$ (0.85 to 10.57) is wrong, because $s_S$ and $s_M$ estimate the population standard deviations.

items.q: Interpret the 95% interval from 0.61 to 10.81 words in context.

why.correct: Name the level, the interval, the parameter (a difference of true means, in the order spaced minus massed) and the context.

options: We are 95% confident that
There is a 95% probability that
95% of the volunteers show that

why.1: The parameter is fixed; confidence describes the method.
why.2: The interval does not describe individual volunteers.

options: the interval from 0.61 to 10.81 words captures
the difference in sample means of 5.71 words falls in
each spaced student recalls 0.61 to 10.81 more words than

why.1: The sample difference is the center; the interval estimates the true difference.
why.2: The interval is about a difference of means, not individual students.

options: the true difference in mean recall (spaced minus massed) for volunteers like these
the difference between the two sample means
the mean recall of spaced students

why.2: The parameter is a difference of two means.

conclude.model: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.61 to 10.81 words captures the true difference in mean recall (spaced minus massed) for volunteers like these.

items.q: Write the expression for a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, using $t^* = 1.996$ (technology df 67.6). Type it as on the exam, for example (a - b) +/- t*sqrt(s^2/m + r^2/n).

mistakes.why: Standard errors do not add. Add the variances 9.8^2/40 and 11.4^2/35 under one square root.
1.96 is z*. With sample standard deviations, use t* from the t distribution: 1.996 here.

items.q: What is the standard error of $\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2$, in minutes?

mistakes.why: That adds the two standard errors, $\frac{9.8}{\sqrt{40}} + \frac{11.4}{\sqrt{35}}$. Add the variances first, then take one square root.
That leaves out the sample sizes. Divide each squared standard deviation by its $n$.

items.q: Construct the 95% confidence interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, in minutes.

why.correct: $4.7 \pm 1.996(2.47) = 4.7 \pm 4.94$, from $-0.23$ to 9.63 minutes ($t^* = 1.996$ at df 67.6; the Table B row for df 60 gives 2.000 and nearly the same interval). On the exam the conservative df, 34, is also accepted: $t^* = 2.032$ gives $-0.33$ to 9.73. Using $z^* = 1.96$ ($-0.15$ to 9.55) is wrong, because $s_1$ and $s_2$ estimate the population standard deviations.

items.q: What does the design of this study allow the researcher to conclude?
options: She can generalize to drivers in the two cities, but not claim the city causes longer commutes
She can claim living in city 1 causes longer commutes
She can generalize her results to commuters in the other large cities in the country
She can conclude nothing, because the samples have different sizes

why.correct: Random sampling allows generalizing; random assignment allows cause-and-effect conclusions. This is an observational study with random samples.
options: Random samples support generalizing to each city's commuters who drive. With no random assignment, a difference could come from other factors, such as distance or road layout.
Cause and effect needs random assignment, which is impossible here.
The samples come from two cities, so results apply to those cities.
Different sample sizes are fine for a two-sample t interval.

items.q: Interpret the 95% confidence level for the commute study's interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ (random samples of 40 and 35 commuters).

why.correct: The level describes the long-run capture rate of the method over repeated pairs of samples of the same sizes.

options: If we took many pairs of random samples of 40 and 35 commuters and built a 95% interval from each pair,
If we surveyed 95% of the commuters in each city,
Since 95% of commute times fall in the interval,

why.1: Confidence is about repeating the sampling, not about surveying most of the population.
why.2: The interval is not built to contain 95% of the data.

options: about 95% of the intervals would capture
about 95% of the differences in sample means would equal
there is a 95% chance this interval captures

why.1: The sample differences vary; the intervals built around them are what capture or miss.
why.2: That sentence is about one interval; the level describes many.

options: the true difference in mean commute time (city 1 minus city 2)
the difference in sample means, 4.7 minutes
the commute time of 95% of drivers

why.1: Every interval captures its own sample difference.
why.2: The intervals estimate a difference of means, not individual times.

conclude.model: If we took many pairs of random samples of 40 and 35 commuters and built a 95% interval from each pair, about 95% of the intervals would capture the true difference in mean commute time (city 1 minus city 2).

items.q: A 95% interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$ is from 2.1 to 6.5. What is the 95% interval for $\mu_B - \mu_A$ from the same data?
options: From 2.1 to 6.5
From 6.5 to 2.1

why.correct: If $\mu_A - \mu_B$ is between 2.1 and 6.5, then $\mu_B - \mu_A$ is between $-6.5$ and $-2.1$.
options: The new parameter is the negative of the old one, so the interval changes sign.
Write the lower end first: $-6.5$ is less than $-2.1$.
Reversing the order of subtraction flips the sign of every value: the interval keeps its width and changes sides of 0.
That reverses the ends without changing signs, and the lower end must come first.

items.q: A two-sample t interval uses samples of $n_1 = 18$ and $n_2 = 25$. What are the conservative degrees of freedom?

why.correct: Conservative degrees of freedom: the smaller of $n_1 - 1 = 17$ and $n_2 - 1 = 24$, so 17. Technology would give a larger, non-integer df.

mistakes.why: $n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 41$ belongs to a method that is not used here. The conservative choice is the smaller $n - 1$.

items.q: From the same data, how does a two-sample t interval with conservative degrees of freedom compare with one using technology degrees of freedom?
options: It is a little narrower
It is a little wider
It is the same width but shifted
It is wider by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$

why.correct: Conservative df never exceed the technology df, so the conservative interval is at least as wide; that is why it is called conservative.
options: The conservative df is smaller, which makes $t^*$ larger, not smaller.
Fewer degrees of freedom give a larger $t^*$ (2.160 at df 13 against 2.057 at df 25.6), so the margin of error grows slightly.
The center, $\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2$, does not depend on df; only the margin of error does.
The difference comes only from $t^*$, which changes by a few percent.

items.q: Which study calls for a two-sample t interval rather than a paired t interval?
options: Battery life of 30 phones of brand A and 30 phones of brand B, chosen at random
Blood pressure of 30 patients measured before and after taking a new medicine for a month
Tread wear on the left and right front tires of 30 cars
Scores of 30 sets of twins, one twin per teaching method

why.correct: Two-sample procedures need two independent groups. Paired procedures are for two linked measurements on each unit.
options: Two separate random samples with no link between a phone of brand A and a phone of brand B.
Each patient gives two linked values: paired.
Left and right tires on the same car are a natural pair.
Twins are matched pairs.

items.q: Why does a confidence interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ use $t^*$ rather than $z^*$?
options: The two samples are of different sizes
Each sample has fewer than 30 observations
The difference in sample means could turn out to be negative
$s_1$ and $s_2$ stand in for the unknown $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$

why.correct: With $s_1$ and $s_2$ estimating $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, the standardized difference follows (approximately) a t distribution.
options: Unequal sample sizes are fine; the reason is the estimated standard deviations.
Large samples use $t^*$ too, whenever the standard deviations are estimated.
The sign of the estimate has nothing to do with the critical value.
Estimating two population standard deviations adds variability, so the critical value comes from a t distribution.

items.q: Which conditions must be checked for a two-sample t interval from two independent random samples? Select all that apply.
options: Each sample is a random sample from its population
Each sample is less than 10% of its population
Each population is normal or each sample has $n \ge 30$, or each sample's graph shows no strong skew or outliers
The two samples have the same size
The two sample standard deviations are about equal
At least 10 successes and 10 failures in each sample

why.correct: Random, 10% and normal/large sample, each checked for both samples.
options: Right: the random condition, for both samples.
Right: checked separately for each sample.
Right: the normal/large sample condition, for both groups.
Sample sizes can differ.
The standard error uses each $s$ separately, so they need not match.
That is the large counts condition for proportions.
